sections.html:
A Freeport seller can list with an agent, sell without one, or accept cash from a buyer who takes the house as it stands. Each route runs through the same village offices, Nassau County recording and New York State transfer tax rules.

With a median owner-occupied home value of $505,900, closing costs, flood questions and unpermitted work can each move the final number. Settling those items before a buyer's attorney finds them is usually the fastest way to a closing date.

Freeport is a village inside the Town of Hempstead on Long Island's South Shore, with larger households than most of New York. Home values run well above upstate cities, and rents are high too. Sunrise Highway (Route 27) crosses the village west to east, and the Meadowbrook State Parkway marks its eastern edge. The Long Island Rail Road reaches Manhattan in roughly 45 minutes, and Freeport Public Schools runs eight schools with one high school.

Many sellers and buyers here work in Spanish as well as English, so make sure disclosures and contracts are explained in a language you read comfortably. Canals such as the Woodcleft Canal, home of the Nautical Mile restaurant strip, reach the Great South Bay and give many homes a marine setting, along with a flood obligation.

For a large share of homes in the southern part of the village, flood zone status is part of the sale. A premises may lie in or beside a FEMA special flood hazard area, and a regular homeowners policy does not cover flood damage. A mortgage holder in a flood zone must carry a separate flood policy.

Freeport takes part in the National Flood Insurance Program and reports a 10% discount on flood premiums. Its Building Department keeps elevation certificates on file and has a certified floodplain manager on staff.

  • Ask the Building Department whether an elevation certificate exists for your address.
  • Look up the flood zone and base flood elevation on FEMA's site or through the village.
  • Remember the substantial improvement rule: if repairs or additions cost 50% or more of a building's market value, the building has to meet new construction standards.

sections.h2: Permits and code checks before listing
sections.html:
The village Building Department administers building, plumbing, electrical and housing codes, and it also regulates multiple residences and unsafe buildings. Permit filings go through the village's OpenGov portal, and structural applications need signed and sealed plans.

A buyer's attorney can ask for proof that finished basements, extensions or extra kitchens were permitted. If something was built without a permit, resolve it before listing so the question does not surface mid-contract.

  • Pull your permit history from the Building Department at 46 N Ocean Avenue.
  • Confirm that any converted space has the proper approvals.
  • Check the village zoning map if the house holds more than one unit.

The village runs more of its own services than most Long Island communities. Its departments include the Assessor, Building, Electric, Water, Public Works, Fire, Police and Recreation, and the Treasurer oversees both the Treasurer's Office and the Tax Office. The Village Clerk handles licenses, permits and village records and works with the Planning Board and Zoning Board.

  • Electric: Freeport operates its own electric department, which has supplied power since 1898, and rates are posted on the village electric site.
  • Water and sewer: the Water Department publishes rates and fees, a conservation and regulations page and an annual water quality report.
  • Sanitation: Public Works posts a pickup schedule by area, so the collection day depends on the street.
  • Emergency alerts: Emergency Management lists hurricane evacuation routes and a CivicReady alert sign-up.

Exemptions handled by the Assessor include senior citizens, limited income disability, clergy, home improvement, non-profit, business development and volunteer firefighters and ambulance workers, plus the STAR program. Ask the Assessor how a change of ownership affects any exemption you hold, and tell the buyer which services are billed separately.

sections.h2: Village tax dates and deed recording
sections.html:
Freeport residents pay a village tax separate from Town of Hempstead, county and school levies. Nassau County runs a different assessment calendar, so call the county for its dates.

  • January 1: village final assessment roll published; the first village bill is due between March 1 and March 31.
  • September 1 to 30: second-half village bills are payable without penalty.
  • October 1: deadline for exemption applications and the taxable status date, by 4:30 p.m. in person.
  • November 1 to the third Tuesday in November: grievance window, closing at 8 p.m.

The Nassau County Clerk records the deed, keeps the official index of real property ownership and offers online land record search. New York's transfer tax is $2 per $500 of price, paid by the seller on a standard sale and reported on Form TP-584 filed with the recording office.

sections.h2: Houses with more than one unit
sections.html:
The Building Department regulates multiple residences, so a house with an extra kitchen or a second unit gets closer attention. Before listing, confirm the zoning map allows the unit count you advertise, and gather the approvals for any conversion. A buyer's attorney will ask, and a gap found late can push back a closing date.

Tell the buyer plainly how the house is used today. A cash buyer may still purchase a property with open questions, but the offer will reflect them, and a clean permit file protects your price. If a flood policy is required, share the zone letter early.

sections.h2: What to have ready for a cash buyer
sections.html:
Bring your permit history, any elevation certificate, your latest village, county and school tax bills, and a list of exemptions you hold. A buyer who sees those papers up front can quote a price without a long inspection period, and your attorney can answer lender questions faster when the file is already organized.

Then ask the village Treasurer and the county for payoff figures. At closing the payoffs come out of your proceeds, the deed is delivered, and the seller or the attorney files the TP-584 return with the recording office.

faqs.q: Does a Freeport seller pay the New York transfer tax?
faqs.a: Yes, on an ordinary sale the seller pays $2 for each $500 of the price, and the TP-584 form goes to the county clerk with the deed. The separate 1% tax on residences of $1 million or more lands on the buyer.

faqs.q: Will flood zone status delay my Freeport closing?
faqs.a: It can if the buyer's lender wants flood insurance quotes first. Collect your flood zone, elevation certificate and any claim history early so the buyer can price a policy without waiting.

faqs.q: Where do I get a permit record for my Freeport house?
faqs.a: Ask the village Building Department, which handles permits and keeps elevation certificates. Its office is at 46 N Ocean Avenue, and permit filings run through the village OpenGov system.

faqs.q: When must I file a grievance on a Freeport assessment?
faqs.a: The village window runs from November 1 until 8 p.m. on the third Tuesday in November, and the application has to be physically in the Assessor's Office by then. A postmark does not count.

faqs.q: Is Freeport its own tax collector?
faqs.a: Partly. The village bills its own tax, and Town of Hempstead, Nassau County and school district taxes arrive separately. Ask the village Treasurer and the county for payoff figures before you close.
